title: App or files
prompt: Pick the agent's next move, then see where it leads:

setup.text: I want to finally start a real knowledge base: notes, projects, ideas, all of it. Should I get one of those notes apps?
The substrate decision comes first, and it's the one that's expensive to reverse: an app's database, or plain files.

options.label: Setting you up with the leading notes app: great editor, sync included, and it has an API I can integrate with for automation.

outcome.text: Can you go through my project notes and update the stale ones?

That needs an API token, three paginated endpoints, and their rate limit. And their API doesn't expose the backlink data at all. What would be grep-and-edit on files is an integration project here. Also worth saying now rather than later: everything you write is accumulating inside their format.

options.verdict: The app optimizes the human editor and walls off everyone else, including your agent. Every future automation pays the API tax, and the notes themselves live in someone else's schema.

options.label: Plain markdown files in a git repo. One folder to start, kebab-case names, frontmatter only where it earns its place. Every tool I have works on it natively, and git gives you history and sync for free.

outcome.text: Go through my project notes and update the stale ones.

Done directly: grepped for last-touched dates, read the four stale ones, proposed edits, committed with a message saying what changed. No integration existed because none was needed: read, grep, move, and version are the native operations on files.

options.verdict: Files made the agent a first-class citizen on day one: the entire tool vocabulary just works, git rides underneath, and the notes will open unchanged in whatever editor or agent exists in ten years.

options.label: Let's design it properly first: I'll draft a folder taxonomy (areas, resources, projects, archives, each with subcategories) so every future note has a correct home before we write anything.

outcome.text: Two weeks later: I've written three notes. Each time I spent five minutes deciding which of the fourteen folders it belonged in.
The taxonomy was designed for notes that didn't exist, and now it charges an admission fee on every thought. Three notes can't tell us the right structure. Thirty could have.

options.verdict: Taxonomy-first is structure ahead of content: a filing decision taxed onto every capture, calibrated on zero data. Two notes that want a home create the home. Structure grows from what accumulates.
